```{r}
#| label: setup

knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6, dpi = 110, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

This guide covers the first step of the `networkflow` pipeline: building the
network. The examples are about bibliographic coupling (documents linked by
the references they share), but the logic applies to any table of links
between two kinds of entities. The guide explains what a projected network is, how the similarity
between two documents is measured, and which choices (measure, threshold,
time windows) shape the network before any cluster is detected. The next
guides cover [finding and reading clusters](finding-and-reading-clusters.html)
and [following clusters over time](following-clusters-over-time.html).

## Why networks?

The volume of documents produced, in science as elsewhere, has grown so
much that no researcher can read a whole corpus. It has become necessary
to group documents on the basis of quantitative measures of their
relations, and to map these groups, their size and their evolution.
Networks are a natural format for this: documents are nodes, linked when
they are related, and clusters of densely linked nodes are the groups.
Citation data are one such measure: by citing, authors say which works they
build on, and the references that articles share reveal groups of works
addressing similar questions with similar tools. Mapping these groups has
become a common tool of the history and sociology of science, including the
history of economics [@claveau2016; @edwards2018; @cherrier2018;
@goutsmedt2023quantitative].

`networkflow` was written for this kind of research. It organises the
analysis as a *pipeline*: building networks from tabular data, detecting
clusters, following them over time, naming and plotting them. Each step is
a function whose choices are explicit arguments, so that they can be
discussed, varied and reported. The functions were developed for, and
used in, studies of European macroeconomics [@goutsmedt2023eer], of the
explanations of the 1970s stagflation [@goutsmedt2021], of the history of
the concept of rationality [@delcey2026] and of the scientific reception
of a report on the environmental impact of livestock [@duluins2026].

## The example data

The examples use a corpus for coupling analysis from @goutsmedt2021: the
books and articles that tried to explain the US stagflation of the 1970s,
published between 1975 and 2013, and the references they cite (the citation
data from which coupling is computed).

```{r}
#| label: data
library(networkflow)
library(ggplot2)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")
nrow(nodes)
head(Ref_stagflation[, c("source_id", "target_id", "target_author", "target_year")])
```

`Nodes_stagflation` has one row per document, `Ref_stagflation` one row per
citation: document `source_id` cites document `target_id`. This is the
typical shape of research data: not a network, but a table of links
between two kinds of entities.

## From a two-mode relation to a network

### Projection

Citations link two sets of entities: citing documents and cited
references. Such a *two-mode*, or *bipartite*, relation can be written as a
matrix $A$ with one row per citing document, one column per reference, and
$a_{ij} = 1$ when document $i$ cites reference $j$. To study the citing
documents, we *project* this relation onto them: two documents are linked
when they cite the same references. The raw strength of the tie is the
number of shared references,

$$
c_{ik} = \sum_j a_{ij} a_{kj} = |R_i \cap R_k|,
$$ {#eq-coupling}

with $R_i$ the bibliography of document $i$. In matrix form (@eq-matrix),
$C$ is the square matrix of the documents whose entry $c_{ik}$ is the
number of references shared by $i$ and $k$:

$$
C = A A^\top.
$$ {#eq-matrix}

This is **bibliographic coupling** [@kessler1963]: two articles are coupled
when their bibliographies overlap. Projecting on the other set gives
**co-citation** [@small1973]: two references are linked when they are
cited together, $A^\top A$. The two networks answer different questions.
Coupling groups the citing documents, and is fixed once they are published:
it maps the *research fronts* of a period. Co-citation groups the cited
works, and evolves as new articles cite them: it maps the *intellectual
base* of a literature as its users see it.

A third relation is often used: **direct citation**, where documents are
linked when one cites the other. It is not a projection (the nodes and the
links concern the same entities), so it needs no function of the package:
a `tbl_graph` built from the table of citations among the documents of the
corpus can be given directly to `add_clusters()` and the following steps.
Which of the three relations represents a field best has been discussed for
a long time, and the answer depends on the criterion. Comparing the
clusters obtained on two million biomedical articles, @boyack2010 found
that bibliographic coupling slightly outperformed co-citation in
representing research fronts, direct citation being the least accurate,
with two measures of accuracy (textual coherence and the concentration of
grants). With another criterion, the concentration of the references of
articles with long bibliographies, @klavans2017 found on the contrary that
direct citation was more accurate than coupling and co-citation.
@rivest2021 found direct citation and a simple label propagation approach on par with a deep learning classification of more than 40 million articles. The relations can also be complementary: for the identification of research topics in computer science, @kleminski2022 find that bibliographic coupling captures more unique information than direct citation or co-citation, and @yan2012 show how the various scholarly networks (coupling, co-citation, co-authorship, co-words) relate to each other. The choice of the relation is therefore a
research choice, not a technical one: coupling is well suited to follow
what a set of documents cites over time (as here), direct citation to
classify very large corpora, co-citation to study the base that a
literature draws on. It is worth checking that the main results of a study
hold with a second relation.

The same logic applies far beyond citations: authors and the papers they
sign (co-authorship), accounts and the hashtags they use, members and the
boards they sit on. `build_network()` projects any such table, given a
`source_id` (the entities that become nodes) and a `target_id` (the
entities that link them).

```{r}
#| label: build
network <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)
network
```

The result is a `tbl_graph` from tidygraph: a node table (the columns of
`nodes`) and an edge table (`from`, `to`, `weight`), which can be
manipulated with [`dplyr`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) verbs and drawn with [`ggraph`](https://ggraph.data-imaginist.com/). Documents without any
shared reference are dropped (`keep_singleton = FALSE`).

### Measuring similarity

Raw counts are a poor measure of similarity because they ignore the length
of the reference lists: the fewer references documents have, the more each
shared reference should count. Normalised measures correct for this (for
instance, in bibliographic coupling, two short notes sharing three
references are probably closer than two long articles sharing three). [`biblionetwork`](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/)
[@goutsmedt2023biblionetwork], which computes the ties, offers five of them,
all available as a `method`. With $R_i$ the set of references of
$i$, $L_i = |R_i|$ the length of its bibliography, $N$ the number of citing
documents and $f_j$ the number of documents citing reference $j$, they fall
into two families.

**Measures that only count the shared references.**

- `"angle"`, the **coupling angle**, the cosine of the angle between the
  two bibliographies seen as vectors of 0 and 1 [@sen1983]:
  $$
  w_{ik} = \frac{|R_i \cap R_k|}{\sqrt{L_i L_k}};
  $$ {#eq-angle}
- `"jaccard"`, the **relative coupling strength** [@sen1983], a
  Jaccard index: the references shared over all the references cited by
  at least one of the two documents,
  $$
  w_{ik} = \frac{|R_i \cap R_k|}{|R_i \cup R_k|}.
  $$ {#eq-jaccard}
  If a note cites 5 references, all cited by an article that cites 50, the
  cosine is $5 / \sqrt{250} \approx 0.32$ and the Jaccard index $5/50 = 0.1$:
  the Jaccard index sees that the article reads much more than the note. It
  is never above the cosine.

**Measures that give less weight to the references that everybody cites**,
in the spirit of the inverse document frequency of text mining.

- `"strength"`, the **coupling strength** [@shen2019]:
  $$
  w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{L_i L_k};
  $$ {#eq-strength}
- `"similarity"`, the **coupling similarity**, the idf-weighted
  cosine of @shen2019, which normalises the same weighted sum by the
  weighted length of each bibliography, $S_i = \sum_{j \in R_i} \log(N / f_j)$,
  as a cosine, so that it lies between 0 and 1 like the angle:
  $$
  w_{ik} = \frac{\sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \log(N / f_j)}{\sqrt{S_i S_k}};
  $$ {#eq-similarity}
- `"vladutz"`, the **Vladutz-Cook formula** [@vladutz1984], the
  ancestor of the coupling strength, whose discount is much steeper
  ($1/f_j$ instead of $\log(N/f_j)$), so that it is almost driven by the
  rarest references:
  $$
  w_{ik} = \frac{4}{L_i + L_k} \sum_{j \in R_i \cap R_k} \frac{1}{f_j}.
  $$ {#eq-vladutz}

The numerator of the coupling strength deserves an explanation. A shared
reference $j$ does not add 1 to the sum but $\log(N/f_j)$: the logarithm of
the inverse of the share of documents citing it. A reference cited by every
document ($f_j = N$) adds $\log(1) = 0$, whereas a reference cited by only
two documents adds $\log(N/2)$, a lot. The sum thus counts shared references
weighted by their rarity, and the denominator $L_i L_k$ then divides it by
the lengths of the two bibliographies, as for the other measures.

Sharing a citation of Taylor's 1993 article on policy rules, cited by 22
documents of the corpus, says less about two explanations of the
stagflation than sharing a reference cited by only two: the second family
encodes this idea. The five measures keep the same pairs (the threshold
applies to the raw count of shared references) and only change their
weights. The `biblionetwork` documentation explains the intuition behind
each of them ([angle](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/reference/coupling_angle.html),
[Jaccard](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/reference/coupling_jaccard.html),
[strength](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/reference/coupling_strength.html),
[similarity](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/reference/coupling_similarity.html),
[Vladutz-Cook](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/reference/coupling_vladutz.html))
and compares them on a corpus in its article
[Comparing measures](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/articles/comparing_measures.html).
There, as in @shen2019, the angle and the Jaccard index give very similar
rankings of the pairs (a Pearson correlation of 0.956 in the corpus of
@shen2019), whereas the Vladutz-Cook formula departs markedly from the
others; it is offered mainly for comparison and replication.

All measures assume that a work has a single identifier. Raw citation
strings do not guarantee it: in `Ref_stagflation`, Friedman's 1968 "The Role
of Monetary Policy" is written with six different author strings and two
titles. Here this is harmless, because the data come with a `target_id`
that the database assigned to each cited work: the 20 citations share the
same identifier, and the documents citing it are coupled. Without such an
identifier, each spelling would be a different reference, and two documents
citing the same work in different ways would not share it. Even with
identifiers, matching is never perfect: about 1.5% of the works of
`Ref_stagflation` (28 of 1,856 distinct titles, after removing punctuation
and comparing with the year) are attached to more than one `target_id`. Check the most
cited references for duplicates before building a network, and clean them
when they matter: the [last guide](beyond-bibliographic-coupling.html)
explains why this matters most for co-citation.

How different are the measures in practice? No need to compare all of
them: we take the coupling angle, its close relative the Jaccard index, and
the coupling similarity, which discounts the common references. We compute
the three networks and compare the weights of the same pairs.

```{r}
#| label: measures
measures <- c("angle", "jaccard", "similarity")
weights <- lapply(measures, function(measure) {
  graph <- build_network(
    nodes = nodes,
    directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
    source_id = "source_id",
    target_id = "target_id",
    method = measure,
    edges_threshold = 1
  )
  ids <- tidygraph::as_tibble(graph, active = "nodes")$source_id
  edges <- tidygraph::as_tibble(graph, active = "edges")
  data.frame(
    pair = paste(pmin(ids[edges$from], ids[edges$to]), pmax(ids[edges$from], ids[edges$to])),
    weight = edges$weight
  )
})
pairs <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "pair"), weights)
names(pairs) <- c("pair", measures)
correlations <- cor(pairs[, measures], method = "spearman")
round(correlations, 3)
```

The three measures keep the same pairs but weight them differently. As
expected, the angle and the Jaccard index rank the pairs almost identically
(a rank correlation of `r sprintf("%.2f", correlations["angle", "jaccard"])`),
while the coupling similarity, which discounts the references that
everybody cites, is further from both (`r sprintf("%.2f", correlations["angle", "similarity"])`
with the angle and `r sprintf("%.2f", correlations["jaccard", "similarity"])` with the Jaccard index). Such a correlation still leaves room for different
clusters at the margin: when the conclusions of a study rest on the exact
composition of a cluster, it is worth checking them with a second measure.
`biblionetwork` has tools to compare measures on a corpus
(`compute_couplings()`, `correlate_weights()`).

### Thresholds

Most pairs of articles in a literature share one or two classic
references. These ties say little, and they make the network dense
(`edges_threshold = 1` links a quarter of all pairs here). Raising the
threshold keeps the pairs that share at least $n$ references:

```{r}
#| label: thresholds
thresholds <- data.frame(threshold = 1:4)
thresholds[c("nodes", "edges", "components")] <- t(sapply(thresholds$threshold, function(n) {
  graph <- build_network(
    nodes = nodes,
    directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
    source_id = "source_id",
    target_id = "target_id",
    method = "similarity",
    edges_threshold = n
  )
  c(igraph::vcount(graph), igraph::ecount(graph), igraph::components(graph)$no)
}))
thresholds
```

Each step removes many edges, but also documents, which no longer share
enough references with any other, and breaks the network into components.
There is no right threshold: it depends on the length of bibliographies
and on the size of the corpus. A threshold of 2 is a common choice for
article corpora; in a corpus of short documents with few references, 1
may be the only option.

### A statistical alternative: backbones

There is a trade-off with computational cost. The backbone approach is,
we think, better, both conceptually a priori and in the networks it
produces a posteriori, but it is very costly and infeasible for large
networks, for which thresholds remain the practical solution. A threshold
is the same for every pair, yet sharing two references means little for
two articles with 150 references each, and a lot for two notes with five.
The *backbone* approach replaces the fixed threshold with a
test [@neal2014]: for each pair, is the number of shared targets larger
than in random bipartite networks that keep some properties of the
observed one? The stochastic degree sequence model (`method = "sdsm"`)
keeps, on average, the number of references of each document and the
number of citations of each reference; the [`backbone`](https://github.com/zpneal/backbone) package
[@domagalski2021; @neal2022] computes the probabilities.

```{r}
#| label: backbone
backbone <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "sdsm",
  alpha = 0.05
)
c(nodes = igraph::vcount(backbone), edges = igraph::ecount(backbone))
```

To see how much the backbone prunes, we compare it with the coupling angle
network (a `biblionetwork` measure) built on the same corpus, with no
threshold and with the threshold of two shared references.

```{r}
#| label: backbone-comparison
angle <- lapply(c(1, 2), function(threshold) {
  build_network(
    nodes = nodes,
    directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
    source_id = "source_id",
    target_id = "target_id",
    method = "angle",
    edges_threshold = threshold
  )
})
n_angle <- sapply(angle, function(graph) c(igraph::vcount(graph), igraph::ecount(graph)))
```

With the coupling angle and a threshold of one shared reference, the
network has `r n_angle[1, 1]` nodes and `r n_angle[2, 1]` edges; with a
threshold of two, `r n_angle[1, 2]` nodes and `r n_angle[2, 2]` edges. The
backbone at the 5% level keeps `r igraph::vcount(backbone)` nodes and
`r igraph::ecount(backbone)` edges: it removes
`r round(100 * (1 - igraph::ecount(backbone) / n_angle[2, 1]))`% of the edges
of the first network and `r round(100 * (1 - igraph::ecount(backbone) / n_angle[2, 2]))`%
of those of the second, and drops the documents that no longer have any
significant tie. It is a much sparser network than the one obtained with a
threshold of two references, which is itself already pruned.

Three things should be kept in mind when reading a backbone.

- The edges are unweighted: an edge only means "more shared references than
  expected under the null model at the 5% level", whatever the number.
- Testing many pairs raises the risk of false positives. A multiple-test
  correction (`backbone_args = list(mtc = "holm")`) addresses it, but
  removes many more edges.
- The backbone is a useful check of a threshold-based network, and the
  better option when the lengths of the reference lists vary a lot, if the
  corpus is small enough to compute it.

### Components

Projected networks often have one large component and small islands.
Community detection and layouts are hard to read on islands, and
`filter_components()` keeps the largest component(s), with a warning if a
large one is dropped:

```{r}
#| label: components
network_2 <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 2
)
main_component <- filter_components(network_2)
c(before = igraph::vcount(network_2), after = igraph::vcount(main_component))
```

Before dropping documents, look at them: a small component may be a
marginal literature that matters to the story.

## Time windows

A network of the whole period is not always what a study needs. Cutting the
corpus into time windows serves three purposes: to study history, that is
the evolution of a literature; to counter the growth of the corpus, since
recent periods contain many more documents and would dominate a single
network; and to avoid detecting communities whose main trait is having been
published at the same period rather than sharing content or a cognitive
relationship. Old works are not irrelevant to recent ones (a physicist
citing Newton is related to him), so this is a choice of the analysis
rather than a necessity. `build_dynamic_networks()` builds one network per time window (it needs a
`time_variable` and a `time_window`: without time, `build_network()` builds
the single network): a window
starting in year $s$ gathers the documents published in
$[s, s + w - 1]$, $w$ being `time_window`, and the network is computed as
if the corpus were limited to them. A new window starts every `window_step`
units. By default, windows follow each other (`window_step = time_window`:
1975-1984, 1985-1994...); with `window_step = 1`, the window slides by one
unit (1975-1984, 1976-1985...); with a step of 5 and a window of 10, each
window shares half of its period with the next one. The step is a way to
trade resolution in time for computing time and for the number of networks
to read.

**Months, weeks and days.** The unit is the one of the time variable when
it is a number. When it is a date (`Date`, `POSIXct`, or an ISO date written
as text such as `"2001-03-15"`), `time_unit` chooses the unit in which
windows are counted: `"year"` (the default), `"quarter"`, `"month"`,
`"week"` or `"day"`. For documents that follow each other quickly, such as
the statements of central banks, the question is how many documents a
window needs to contain: a network of twenty documents has no structure to
detect. With monthly data, a window of 12 months sliding by 3 gives a
yearly window every quarter:

```r
build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = statements,            # one row per statement, with a `date` column
  directed_edges = citations,
  source_id = "statement_id",
  target_id = "reference_id",
  time_variable = "date",
  time_unit = "month",
  time_window = 12,
  window_step = 3,
  method = "angle"
)
```

Windows are named after their first and last unit (`"2001-01 to 2001-12"`
for months, `"2001-Q1 to 2001-Q4"` for quarters, `"1975-1984"` for years).
The column of the user is never modified.

```{r}
#| label: dynamic
networks <- build_dynamic_networks(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  time_variable = "source_year",
  time_window = 10,
  window_step = 1,
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1,
  filter_components = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)
length(networks)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-window-size
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-alt: >
#|   Number of documents in the main component of each ten-year window, from
#|   1975-1984 to 2004-2013: high in the first windows, very low for windows
#|   centred on the late 1980s, and rising again from the mid-1990s.
window_sizes <- data.frame(
  window = names(networks),
  start = as.integer(substr(names(networks), 1, 4)),
  nodes = sapply(networks, igraph::vcount)
)
ggplot(window_sizes, aes(start, nodes)) +
  geom_col(fill = scico::scico(1, palette = "batlow", begin = 0.3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = window_sizes$start[seq(1, nrow(window_sizes), by = 5)],
    labels = window_sizes$window[seq(1, nrow(window_sizes), by = 5)],
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.01))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Window", y = "Documents in the main component") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

The size of the windows tells a story of its own: the stagflation was
widely debated in the late 1970s and early 1980s, interest faded after the
mid-1980s, and a new literature on it emerged in the 1990s, the pattern
that @goutsmedt2021 describes. It also
warns about a technical limit: windows centred on the late 1980s contain
about ten documents, too few for their clusters to mean much. The choice
of the window is substantive. It should be long enough for each network
to have enough documents to show a structure, and short enough for
changes to be visible. Sliding windows smooth the evolution (consecutive
networks share 90% of their period here) and make clusters easier to
follow; successive windows give independent snapshots.

## What comes next

The networks are ready for [community detection](finding-and-reading-clusters.html).
Each choice made here (measure, threshold, window) changes them: report
these choices, and check that the main results hold under reasonable
alternatives.
